title: Objective Recoil and Complementarity in the Single-Atom Einstein–Bohr Experiment: A Physical–Observation Dual-Axis Formulation
content: Nearly a century after the 1927 Solvay exchange, the Einstein–Bohr recoiling-slit experiment has been realized with a single optically trapped 87Rb atom. The atom is light enough for one scattered photon to leave a resolvable motional record, and sufficiently controllable for the overlap of the two opposite recoil states to be tuned across the quantum regime. The resulting visibility curve is commonly read as an experimental confirmation of Bohr. That reading is correct, but incomplete: the same experiment also makes visible the objective recoil carrier on which Einstein’s argument rested. We develop a physical–observation dual-axis formulation in which the photon path x ∈ X and the atomic motional state s ∈ S enter as irreducible state coordinates of the observed fact r = F(x,s). The joint photon atom state then gives a complex cross-axis coherence kernel γS = ⟨s−|s+⟩. Its modulus is the photon visibility, its phase transports the fringe origin, and the distinguishability of the same two recoil records supplies the available path information. For a Gaussian motional ground state the construction yields V = exp(−2η2), with η = hk /(2∆p), reproducing the dependence tested in the experiment. We also prove that, whenever controlled atomic states generate different complex kernels at fixed photon preparation, no photon-only response map can represent the complete phase-resolved family of observations. Standard quantum mechanics satisfies this requirement by retaining the composite state; the dual-axis formulation makes its observational structure explicit. The resulting synthesis is precise: Einstein was right about the reality and physical location of the recoil record, while Bohr was right about the bound governing its coexistence with interference. Neither the necessity of a classical apparatus cut nor the completeness of quantum single-event dynamics follows from the experiment. Phase-sensitive and closed-loop extensions are proposed to probe the complex cross-axis response beyond visibility alone.
